unesco.title: Khorazm dance, Lazgi
unesco.description: The movements of Khorazm dance, Lazgi encapsulate human creativity by reflecting the sounds and phenomena of surrounding nature, feelings of love and happiness. Initially associated with the Khorazm Region, Khorazm dance, Lazgi has since become widespread in Uzbekistan. Paintings of the dance can be found in the archaeological site of Tuproqqala, in the Khorazm Region, testifying to its centuries-old roots. Informed by the social life and activities of the local communities, Lazgi dance represents real life in all its movements. During the dance, all the musicians, singers and dance performers act in a harmonized way, and the lyrics of the songs are mainly devoted to glorifying love and kindness. Two types of dance exist: the ‘scenery’ dance and the interpretive improvised form. While the scenery dance represents these feelings through concrete movements, its interpretation focuses on improvisation as the rhythm and dance movements become more dynamic with changeable actions. The melody and dance of Lazgi are so attractive that spectators start dancing voluntarily. Khorazm Dance, Lazgi is a key form of self-expression and is transmitted across the generations through the creation of new versions of performances. It is performed during national holidays and folk festivities in scenery forms, as well as in the daily-based interpretation form during community and family events.

profile.name: Lazgi
profile.tagline: A rhythmic, high-energy dance from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan.
profile.insight: Legend holds that Lazgi originated when divine music enchanted a soul, causing it to enter a clay body, starting with the fingers and toes before the entire human form came to life.
profile.profile: Lazgi is a traditional dance and musical form from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan, characterized by its energetic progression and intricate hand movements. It begins with slow, deliberate gestures—starting from the fingers and wrists—before accelerating into a dynamic, high-tempo performance. Recognized by UNESCO as an intangible cultural heritage, the dance is performed in both structured, scenery-based forms and spontaneous, improvisational styles. It remains a central element of Khorezmian social life, reflecting themes of love, nature, and human vitality.
profile.profile_long: Lazgi is a foundational folk dance and musical tradition originating from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan. It is defined by a distinct progression: the performance begins with slow, isolated movements of the fingers, wrists, and elbows, gradually involving the entire body as the rhythm intensifies. This structure mirrors local oral traditions, which describe the dance as the physical manifestation of a soul entering a clay body, brought to life by divine music. Archaeological evidence of the dance, including ancient paintings, has been discovered at the site of Tuproqqala, indicating that the form has deep historical roots in the region. In modern practice, Lazgi is categorized into two primary modes: the 'scenery' dance, which utilizes concrete, choreographed movements to represent feelings of love and happiness, and an interpretive, improvisational form that allows for dynamic, spontaneous expression. The music typically follows a 6/8 meter and consists of a short introduction followed by three distinct parts. As the music progresses, the tempo increases, leading to a highly energetic finale that often ends abruptly. The dance is deeply embedded in the social fabric of Uzbekistan, performed during national holidays, family celebrations, and community festivities. Its popularity has led to the development of various regional styles, including Qayroq, Dutor, Surnay, Masxaraboz, Saroy, Changak, Khiva, and Garmon Lazgi. Throughout the 20th century, artists such as Komiljon Otaniyozov, Tamara Khanum, and Mukarrama Turgunbayeva played significant roles in modernizing and promoting the dance on both national and international stages. Today, the form continues to evolve through new lyrical yalla versions and ballet adaptations, maintaining its status as a vital expression of Khorezmian culture.

sections.origins_and_history: Oral traditions link the dance to the creation of the human form, where music acts as the catalyst for life. Archaeological evidence of the dance is found at the Tuproqqala site in the Khorezm region.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance begins with slow, isolated movements of the fingers, wrists, and elbows. As the music accelerates, the dancer incorporates bent-leg stances, shoulder movements, and more complex, rapid footwork and hand gestures.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed in a 6/8 meter. It consists of a small introduction followed by three parts. Instruments include the dutar, surnay, garmon, and qayroq (clappers).
sections.costume_and_setting: Not described in sources beyond the mention of bells attached to the hands of the dancers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at national holidays, folk festivities, and family or community events. It is used to express love, happiness, and the phenomena of nature.
sections.notable_figures: Tamara Khanum, Mukarrama Turgunbayeva, Gavhar Matyakubova, Komiljon Otaniyozov, Abdusharif Otajonov, Matniyoz Yusupov.
sections.regional_variants: Eight types exist: Qayroq, Dutor, Surnay, Masxaraboz, Saroy, Changak, Khiva, and Garmon Lazgi.

basic_steps: Begin with slow, isolated finger movements.
Progress to wrist and elbow rotations.
Engage the torso and shoulders while maintaining bent-leg posture.
Increase speed and complexity of footwork in sync with the music.
teaching.rhythm: 6/8 meter with a lively, accelerating tempo.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with slow, controlled isolation of the upper body.

music_profile.vocal_style: Includes yalla versions with lyrics; traditional instrumental versions also common.
music_profile.sound_description: A rhythmic, driving sound characterized by the interplay of traditional strings and wind instruments, building in intensity and speed.

movement_profile.footwork: Not described in sources beyond 'complex movements'.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Intricate movements of fingers, wrists, and elbows; hands may feature bells.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Involved as the dance progresses and tempo increases.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Starts slow and deliberate, accelerating to an intense, rapid pace.

signature_moves.name: Finger and wrist isolation
signature_moves.description: The initial, slow movement of fingers and wrists that signals the start of the dance.

episode_brief.logline: Discover the ancient Khorezmian dance that brings the human form to life through the power of rhythm.

The transition to high-energy, complex movement.
The role of UNESCO in preserving the tradition.
Modern interpretations and the influence of Komiljon Otaniyozov.

drills: Maintaining bent-leg posture while moving arms.

episode_brief.instructor_persona: A traditional Khorezmian dancer with a focus on the history and spiritual connection of the movement.
episode_brief.music_cue: A traditional Surnay Lazgi recording that begins slowly and builds to a fast tempo.

connections.name: Khorezm folk dance
connections.note: Lazgi is the most prominent form within the broader Khorezm folk tradition.

claims.text: Lazgi was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on December 13, 2019.
claims.quote: Lazgi was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity under the name “Khorezm dance – Lazgi” on December 13, 2019.

claims.text: The dance begins with slow movements of the fingers and wrists before the whole body engages.
claims.quote: The dance starts with slow and simple movements; first the fingers, wrists, elbows and then the whole body comes to life.

claims.text: The music is performed in a 6/8 meter.
claims.quote: It is performed in a 6/8 meter with a lively rhythm.

claims.text: Archaeological evidence of the dance exists at the Tuproqqala site.
claims.quote: Paintings of the dance can be found in the archaeological site of Tuproqqala, in the Khorazm Region, testifying to its centuries-old roots.

claims.text: Oral tradition suggests the dance represents the soul entering the body.
claims.quote: It is said that it expresses the process of the soul entering the body, or that it was created to help stay warm in the cold climate.
